501.event_title: China selects its officials by imperial examination
501.event: From the Sui and Tang dynasties onward, Chinese governments increasingly filled official posts through competitive written examinations on the classical Chinese texts rather than by birth or recommendation alone. Under the Ming and Qing the examinations ran in three levels, at county, provincial and capital level, and the highest degree, the jinshi, made a candidate eligible for high office. The system lasted until it was abolished in 1905.
501.explanation: For well over a thousand years one of the world's largest states refused to hand out office until candidates had been examined, and the examinations were meant to test character as well as learning.
501.tie_back: The kural insists that a person be tested before being trusted with office, and imperial China built that principle into a permanent state institution.
501._accuracy_note: Captures the principle of examining before appointing, but the examinations tested learning, not the four specific temptations (virtue, wealth, pleasure, fear) the kural names.

502.event_title: Lord Carrington resigns as Foreign Secretary
502.event: Three days after Argentina invaded the Falkland Islands, Peter Carington, 6th Baron Carrington, resigned as British Foreign Secretary together with two junior ministers. In his resignation letter he said that much of the criticism was unfounded, but that he had been responsible for the conduct of the policy and thought it right to resign. A later official inquiry did not find him at fault, and his acceptance of responsibility was widely praised.
502.explanation: A minister of old family and long service chose to give up high office rather than let a failure of his department rest on anyone else, an unusually clear example of personal honour in politics.
502.tie_back: The kural asks for someone of good family who dreads any stain on his name, and Carrington's resignation shows that sense of shame acting as a safeguard of public trust.
502._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of family standing joined to a sense of honour that fears blame, though the kural is about choosing such a person rather than about the person's own resignation.

503.event_title: Vesalius corrects Galen's anatomy in the Fabrica
503.place: Padua, Republic of Venice (now Italy); printed in Basel, Switzerland
503.event: Andreas Vesalius, professor of anatomy at Padua, published De humani corporis fabrica in 1543, based on his own dissections of human bodies. It corrected many errors in the work of Galen, the Greek physician whose anatomy had been treated as authoritative for some 1,300 years. Many of Galen's mistakes came from the fact that he had described human anatomy largely from dissections of animals.
503.explanation: Even the most revered authority in medicine turned out, on close examination, to have hidden gaps in his knowledge.
503.tie_back: The kural says that even the learned and seemingly flawless will rarely be found free of ignorance when closely examined, and Galen's errors show exactly that.
503._accuracy_note: A close fit to the claim that close examination finds some ignorance even in the most learned, though it concerns a writer's work rather than a candidate for office.

504.event_title: General Groves chooses Oppenheimer to lead Los Alamos
504.place: Washington, D.C. and Los Alamos, New Mexico, United States
504.event: General Leslie Groves, head of the Manhattan Project, chose the physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer to direct its new weapons laboratory even though Oppenheimer had almost no administrative experience, had not won a Nobel Prize, and faced security objections over past left-wing associations. Groves ordered that his clearance be issued, calling him essential to the project. Groves later wrote that he had never felt it was a mistake to select and clear Oppenheimer for the post.
504.explanation: Groves openly listed the candidate's drawbacks and still judged that his breadth of knowledge and drive outweighed them.
504.tie_back: The kural tells us to weigh a person's virtues against his faults and judge by whichever prevails, which is what Groves did.
504._accuracy_note: A documented case of consciously weighing known strengths against known weaknesses before appointing someone.

505.event_title: Bonaparte creates the Legion of Honour
505.event: As First Consul, Napoleon Bonaparte created the Legion of Honour by a law of 19 May 1802. It was an order of merit for both military and civil service, open to recipients without regard to birth or religion. It remains France's highest order of merit.
505.explanation: In a society that had long rewarded noble birth, the state chose to honour people for what they had actually done.
505.tie_back: The kural calls deeds the touchstone of greatness and meanness, and the Legion of Honour made deeds, not birth, the test for honour.
505._accuracy_note: Fits the idea that deeds alone show a person's worth, but an award system recognises greatness and does not show the 'meanness' half of the kural.

506.event_title: The Praetorian Guard sells its support to Didius Julianus
506.event: After the Praetorian Guard killed the emperor Pertinax in 193, two men sought its backing for the throne, and the wealthy senator Didius Julianus won by promising the soldiers the larger cash payment. The Guard then proclaimed him emperor. Julianus ruled only about two months before he was deposed when Septimius Severus marched on Rome.
506.explanation: Soldiers whose loyalty was tied to no ruler and no community gave the empire to whoever paid most, with no apparent concern for the disgrace.
506.tie_back: The kural warns against trusting people with no ties, since having no attachments they feel no shame at blame, and the Guard's sale of its support is a stark case.
506._accuracy_note: Next-best: the Guard was cut loose from any loyalty and unashamed, but the kural's reason (lack of kin) does not literally apply, and ancient accounts of an 'auction' may be exaggerated.

507.event_title: Charles IV makes the guardsman Manuel Godoy his chief minister
507.event: Manuel Godoy, a young officer of the royal bodyguard and a protege of Queen Maria Luisa, was raised by King Charles IV to the highest offices and made chief minister in 1792 at about the age of 25. His rule was marked by costly wars, financial strain and growing unpopularity. In March 1808 the Revolt of Aranjuez forced his dismissal and the abdication of Charles IV, which opened the way for Napoleon to take control of Spain.
507.explanation: A government handed to a royal favourite without proven ability ended in the fall of the king himself.
507.tie_back: The kural warns that trusting unqualified people merely because one is fond of them brings every kind of folly, and Godoy's career shows the result.
507._accuracy_note: A textbook case of appointment by royal favour rather than ability leading to disaster, though historians credit Godoy with a few achievements such as the Peace of Basel.

508.event: King Lobengula of the Ndebele signed a concession with agents of Cecil Rhodes led by Charles Rudd, believing he was granting limited mining rights. The written document gave the grantees exclusive rights to all metals and minerals in his kingdoms, and Lobengula later repudiated it and sent envoys to London to protest. The British government accepted the concession in 1889 and used it to charter the British South Africa Company, which went on to take over his kingdom.
508.explanation: Trust placed in outsiders without fully examining what was being signed cost the king his realm and his people their land for generations.
508.tie_back: The kural warns that trusting a stranger without examination brings endless sorrow even on one's descendants, which is what followed this signature.
508._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation: unexamined trust in outsiders, followed by lasting harm to the ruler's line and people.

509.event_title: The Soviet Union selects Yuri Gagarin for Vostok 1
509.place: Moscow and Star City, Soviet Union (now Russia)
509.event: In 1960 the Soviet Union chose its first group of 20 cosmonaut candidates from among military pilots after extensive medical and psychological testing. After further training and examinations, managers ranked Yuri Gagarin first, with Gherman Titov as his backup, and on 12 April 1961 Gagarin made the first human spaceflight. The candidates themselves had voted overwhelmingly for Gagarin as the one they wanted to fly first.
509.explanation: No one was trusted with the first human spaceflight until he had been examined repeatedly, and the trust was then given in full.
509.tie_back: The kural says to trust no one without examining him and, once examined, to trust him in what he is fit for, as the Soviet selection did.
509._accuracy_note: A clear case of exhaustive examination followed by full trust in a specific role.

510.event_title: Admiral Yi Sun-sin is removed from command
510.event: In 1597, during the Japanese invasions of Korea, Admiral Yi Sun-sin, who had already won a series of naval victories, was falsely accused, arrested and reduced to the rank of a common soldier. His replacement, Won Gyun, led the fleet into a defeat at Chilcheollyang in which almost all of its warships were lost. Yi was then restored to command and, with only about a dozen ships, won the Battle of Myeongnyang in October 1597.
510.explanation: A government that doubted its proven commander lost nearly its entire navy before turning back to him.
510.tie_back: The kural warns that doubting someone already tested and trusted brings endless trouble, and Korea's naval disaster of 1597 shows it.
510._accuracy_note: Almost exactly the second error the kural names: suspicion toward a proven servant, with severe consequences.
